concept.technique_name: fragment detection via missing main verb
concept.sub_category: Sentence Structure - subject/verb and participial modifiers

examples.problem_statement: Multiple choice with one correct answer; answer (A) repeats the original sentence, and only two choices are offered. Watch for sentence-structure issues. Sentence: "Some of the earliest computer games designed to involve many players at once and first developed before the widespread availability of high-speed internet connections." (A) Some of the earliest computer games designed to involve many players at once and first developed before the widespread availability of high-speed internet connections. (B) First developed before the widespread availability of high-speed internet connections, some of the earliest computer games were designed to involve many players at once.

solution.operation: Search choice (A) for a conjugated main verb
solution.result: the only verb-like words found are designed and developed
solution.description: Read the original sentence hunting for a working verb attached to the subject; the book points to designed and developed as the only candidates.

solution.operation: Classify designed and developed as participles, not verbs
solution.result: both are modifiers that only masquerade as verbs
solution.description: Test the two candidates: the book identifies them as participles, so they modify the subject rather than serve as its verb.

solution.operation: Conclude (A) has no main verb at all
solution.result: choice (A) is a sentence fragment
solution.description: With every verb candidate ruled out as a modifier, the book declares the sentence verbless and therefore a fragment, so (A) is wrong.

solution.operation: Check choice (B) for the missing main verb
solution.result: (B) supplies the main verb were designed
solution.description: Look at the alternative: the book notes (B) fixes the mistake by turning the participle into the main verb were designed, giving the sentence a complete core.

key_reminders: A participle such as designed or developed is a modifier, not a main verb.
A sentence with no main verb is a fragment, no matter how long it is.
The fix for a verbless sentence is to convert one participle into a working verb (were designed).
common_mistakes: Reading designed and developed as the sentence's verbs because they follow the subject directly.
Being reassured by the sentence's length and the and joining the two participles, and so missing that nothing predicates the subject.

concept.technique_name: logical-clue text completion across linked blanks

examples.problem_statement: Select one entry for each blank from the corresponding column of choices; fill all blanks in the way that best completes the text. "The reason minimum temperatures are going up more rapidly than maximums may involve cloud cover and evaporative cooling. Clouds tend to keep the days cooler by reflecting sunlight, and the nights warmer by (i) ______ loss of heat from Earth's surface. Greater amounts of moisture in the soil from additional precipitation and cloudiness (ii) ______ the daytime temperature increases because part of the solar energy is (iii) ______ the evaporation of that moisture." Blank (i): A inhibiting, B exacerbating, C replicating. Blank (ii): D augment, E mask, F restrain. Blank (iii): G intensified by, H unrelated to, I used up in.

solution.operation: Read the second sentence: clouds make nights warmer by acting on heat loss
solution.result: Blank (i) needs a word meaning preventing or slowing heat loss, so inhibiting
solution.description: Follow the book's logic that less heat lost means more warmth, so the blank must slow heat loss; exacerbating means the opposite and replicating makes no sense here.

solution.operation: Use the first sentence: daytime highs rise less rapidly than nighttime lows
solution.result: Blank (ii) needs a verb of moderation, so restrain
solution.description: Apply the contrast the passage opens with: the moisture must hold back the daytime rises, which restrain expresses; augment means increase, and mask would wrongly claim the measurements hide real increases.

solution.operation: Read the because clause explaining how the daytime increases are restrained
solution.result: Blank (iii) needs a phrase diverting solar energy, so used up in
solution.description: Follow the causal word because: the clause must show evaporation lessening or diverting the solar energy that warms the surface, which used up in does; intensified by and unrelated to give no such lessening connection.

solution.operation: Combine the three selections into the completed text
solution.result: inhibiting (Choice A), restrain (Choice F), used up in (Choice I)
solution.description: Assemble the three choices and confirm the passage now reads as one consistent explanation of why minimums rise faster than maximums.

examples.answer: Choice A: inhibiting; Choice F: restrain; Choice I: used up in

key_reminders: Less heat lost from the surface means warmer nights, so the blank must slow that loss.
The opening comparison (minimums rising faster than maximums) fixes the direction of the daytime blank as moderation.
The word because signals that the final clause must explain the restraint, via energy diverted into evaporation.
common_mistakes: Choosing exacerbating for Blank (i) by attaching the word to the heat rather than to the loss of heat.
Choosing mask for Blank (ii), which would say the measurements hide real increases - an idea the passage never supports.
Choosing intensified by for Blank (iii), which reverses the energy flow the because clause requires.

concept.technique_name: division by flag digits with quotient adjustment

config.operation: cross product sum subtracted from the gross dividend

examples.problem_statement: Using the Division Algorithm with Flag Digits technique: a multi-step division using flag digits and quotient adjustment rules. Given: initial division 20 \div 5 = 4 remainder 0; adjusted quotient at step 3 gives Q2 = 3, R2 = 5; cross product at step 4 is 2\times 3 + 1\times 4 = 10; net dividend at step 4 is 53 - 10 = 43; division at step 4 is 43 \div 5 = 8 remainder 3; cross product at step 5 is 3\times 4 + 2\times 8 = 28; net dividend at step 5 is 38 - 28 = 10; division at step 5 is 10 \div 5 = 2 remainder 0. Reproduce the method step by step and state the final result.

solution.result: adjusted step-3 quotient Q2 = 3 with remainder R2 = 5
solution.description: The initial division left a zero remainder in the middle of the working, so apply the rule that decrements the quotient by 1 and recomputes the remainder before carrying on.

solution.result: net dividend 43, giving Q3 = 8 and R3 = 3
solution.description: Take the gross dividend 53, subtract the cross product of the flag digits 2 and 1 with the quotient digits 3 and 4, then divide the resulting net dividend by the divisor 5.

solution.result: net dividend 10, giving Q4 = 2 and R4 = 0
solution.description: Repeat the same subtraction on the next column: from the gross dividend 38 remove the cross product of the paired digits 3, 4 and 2, 8, then divide the net dividend 10 by 5.

solution.result: adjusted final quotient digit 1 with remainder 5
solution.description: The remainder came out zero again, so apply the zero-remainder rule a second time: decrement the quotient digit and recompute the remainder to close the working.

examples.answer: Final quotient digits: 1, 3, 8, 1 with corresponding remainders at each step.

key_reminders: Net dividend = gross dividend minus the cross product of the flag digits with the quotient digits already found.
A zero remainder in the middle of the working triggers the adjustment rule: decrement that quotient digit by 1 and recompute the remainder.
Each column's division is performed on the net dividend, never on the gross dividend.
common_mistakes: Dividing the gross dividend (53 or 38) by 5 without first subtracting the cross product.
Leaving Q2 = 4 and Q4 = 1 unadjusted when the remainder comes out 0, which breaks the remaining columns.
Pairing the wrong digits in the cross product at step 5 (3\times 4 + 2\times 8, not 3\times 8 + 2\times 4).

examples.problem_statement: Select one entry for each blank from the corresponding column of choices; fill all blanks in the way that best completes the text. "Statements presented as fact in a patent application are (i) ______ unless a good reason for doubt is found. The invention has only to be deemed 'more likely than not' to work in order to receive initial approval. And, although thousands of patents are challenged in court for other reasons, no incentive exists for anyone to expend effort (ii) ______ the science of an erroneous patent. For this reason the endless stream of (iii) ______ devices will continue to yield occasional patents." Blank (i): A presumed verifiable, B carefully scrutinized, C considered capricious. Blank (ii): D corroborating, E advancing, F debunking. Blank (iii): G novel, H bogus, I obsolete.

solution.operation: Start at Blank (ii), whose sentence is about challenges to patents
solution.result: debunking is the only choice concerned with challenging a patent
solution.description: Use the third sentence as the anchor the book chooses: it discusses challenges, and of the options only debunking attacks a patent, while corroborating and advancing suggest support.

solution.result: bogus fits the devices that nonetheless get patents
solution.description: Since the preceding sentence explains why nobody bothers debunking bad science, the following sentence must name the devices that slip through, which bogus does.

solution.operation: Return to Blank (i) with the paragraph's point now fixed
solution.result: presumed verifiable
solution.description: The first sentence must also help explain how bogus devices get patents, which works only if applications are taken at face value - neither dismissed as capricious nor carefully scrutinized.

solution.operation: Combine the three selections into the completed paragraph
solution.result: presumed verifiable (Choice A), debunking (Choice F), bogus (Choice H)
solution.description: Assemble the choices and check the paragraph now reads as one explanation of the odd aspect of the patent process it set out to describe.

examples.answer: Choice A: presumed verifiable; Choice F: debunking; Choice H: bogus

key_reminders: Fill the blank whose sentence carries the clearest clue first, then let it constrain the others.
The paragraph exists to explain an odd feature of the patent process, so every blank must serve that explanation.
For this reason signals that the last sentence is a consequence of the sentence before it.
common_mistakes: Filling Blank (i) first and choosing carefully scrutinized, which contradicts the 'more likely than not' standard described next.
Choosing corroborating or advancing for Blank (ii), which support rather than challenge a patent.
Choosing novel for Blank (iii), a positive word that undoes the paragraph's point about erroneous patents.

concept.technique_name: minute-by-minute rate accumulation with changing rates

chain: fractional part of the next minute

examples.problem_statement: Three water pipes A, B and C are all used to fill a container. They can fill the container individually in 6 minutes, 12 minutes and 18 minutes respectively. All three pipes were opened simultaneously. However, pipes A and B supplied water at 2/3 of their normal rates for the first minute, after which they supplied water at the normal rate. Pipe C supplied water at half its normal rate for the first 3 minutes, after which it supplied water at its normal rate. In how much time (in minutes and to the closest second) would the container be filled?

solution.operation: Carry forward the unfilled volume at the start of the third minute
solution.result: 57 litres remain to be filled
solution.description: Begin from the position the book states after the first two minutes of reduced-rate filling: 57 litres of the container are still empty as the third minute starts.

solution.result: 30 litres are filled during the third minute
solution.description: Add the three pipes' contributions for the third minute, in which C is still on its reduced rate, to get the minute's filling rate.

solution.result: 27 litres unfilled at the start of the fourth minute
solution.description: Subtract what the third minute delivered from the 57 litres outstanding to find how much is still missing when the fourth minute begins.

solution.result: 33 litres per minute in the fourth minute
solution.description: Recompute the combined rate for the fourth minute, now that C has switched to its normal rate, so its share rises from 3 to 6.

solution.result: 9/11 of the fourth minute is used
solution.description: Divide the 27 litres still needed by the fourth minute's rate of 33 litres per minute to get the fraction of that minute actually required.

solution.operation: 3 + 9/11 minutes converted to minutes and seconds
solution.result: 3\frac{9}{11} minutes
solution.description: Add the fraction of the fourth minute to the three complete minutes already elapsed and express the total to the nearest second.

key_reminders: When rates change part-way, work minute by minute and recompute the combined rate for each minute.
Pipe C's rate doubles from the fourth minute onward, since its half-rate period covers only the first 3 minutes.
The final partial minute is the leftover volume divided by that minute's rate.
common_mistakes: Keeping C at 3 litres per minute in the fourth minute instead of raising it to 6 when the reduced-rate period ends.
Treating the leftover 27 litres as a whole extra minute instead of the fraction 9/11 of one.
Rounding 9/11 of a minute carelessly rather than converting it to 49 seconds.
